name: North Korea
card_headline: North Korea expands its Yongbyon enrichment plant and deepens ties with Russia and China, while Trump left the APEC summit without meeting Kim.
card_summary: North Korea is a nuclear-armed one-party state that says talks with Washington require recognition of its nuclear status. [10] The IAEA reports a new extension at the Yongbyon enrichment plant. [5] Pyongyang sends troops and shells to Russia, and Xi Jinping visited in June. [20][4] The Bank of Korea estimates 3.5 percent growth in 2025, yet rice costs about five times its May 2024 price. [29][30] Public executions are reported to be rising. [36]
card_local: Local sourcing is thin by necessity: Daily NK reports rice at 38,200 won per kilogram in Pyongyang and ASIAPRESS reports grain controls tightening, both from anonymous contacts that cannot be checked. [1][25]
card_international: AP reported Xi's June visit and the IAEA's November finding on Yongbyon, and Euronews reported that Trump left China on 19 November without meeting Kim. [4][5][3]
card_scholar: The MSMT's September report estimates 35,600 to 101,280 North Korean workers abroad, and 38 North's analysts expect weapons production to continue. [6][7]
context_md: The Workers' Party held its Ninth Congress in February 2026, the first in five years, and Kim Jong Un was re-elected general secretary. [10] In June 2024 Russia and North Korea signed a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty, and in April 2025 Pyongyang acknowledged sending troops to fight in Kursk. [20] The UN Panel of Experts that monitored sanctions ended in April 2024 after a Russian veto, and an 11-government team now does that work outside the Council. [44] North Korea has not allowed IAEA inspectors in for years. [5] A constitution text that surfaced in South Korea treats the South as a separate state. [11] Reporting from inside the country is impossible for outsiders, and what reaches the public comes from state media, exile outlets and defector testimony. [42]

sections.title: Kim has written the two-state line into law and priced talks at recognition as a nuclear state
sections.body_md:
The Ninth Congress of the Workers' Party opened on 19 February 2026 with about 5,000 representatives, and Kim told them the country had overcome its worst difficulties of the past five years. [9] North Korean media published only a summary of his report, so outside analysts work from partial text. [7] Michael Madden of 38 North reads the personnel changes as a focus on domestic economic policy, and Daily NK says the Party Secretariat grew from eight to twelve members. [7][8]

Kim said on the congress's last day that bilateral talks with the United States require recognition of North Korea as a nuclear-armed state, that denuclearization is not possible, and that there will be no negotiations with South Korea. [10] A constitution text that surfaced in South Korea in May drops the unification framework and treats the South as a separate state. North Korean state media never published it in full, and 38 North says it appears to reflect revisions made in October 2024, January 2025 and March 2026. [11]

Relations with the South have hardened at the border. On 21 September two explosions near the western DMZ wounded three South Korean soldiers, and the UN Command said a joint investigation with Seoul found an active North Korean anti-personnel mine on the southern side. Kim Yo Jong called Seoul's assessment a "conspiratorial farce", and North Korea denies planting mines. [48] South Korea's intelligence service has told lawmakers that Kim's daughter Ju Ae has entered "the stage of being designated as successor". That assessment reached the public second hand, and the report carries no response from Pyongyang. [12]

lenses.local: Daily NK's analysis of the congress, drawn from its own report, calls the result "Kim Jong Un regime 2.0" and says military figures Ri Pyong Chol and Pak Jong Chon lost Party standing. [8]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera, citing Yonhap, noted that Kim did not mention relations with the US or South Korea in his opening speech. [9]
lenses.scholar: Vann Van Diepen expects nuclear weapons production to continue, and Gyeong Seob Oh sees no concrete economic reforms or sanctions relief in the five-year plan. [7]

sections.title: The nuclear program keeps growing: a larger Yongbyon plant, a nuclear-minded navy and tests every few days
sections.body_md:
IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi told the agency's board on 18 November that a further extension to the original Yongbyon enrichment facility had been under construction since mid-September and was externally complete by late October. He called the expansion "extremely worrying". Inspectors have been barred for years, so the IAEA works from satellite imagery and open sources, and the report gives no output figures. [5] Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui said the week before that nuclear weapons are the strongest guarantee of sovereignty. [5] South Korea's president, Lee Jae Myung, told the New York Times in September that the North is producing or can produce 10 to 20 nuclear weapons a year, and urged sanctions relief in exchange for a freeze. [13]

Testing has picked up after a quiet 2025, when 38 North counted about 15 ballistic missile launches against 41 in 2024. [15] On 20 September two launches traveled about 280 and 370 miles, and KCNA called it a new-type weapon. [13] On 4 November Seoul detected several missiles from the Sondok area, and KCNA said Pyongyang had tested an advanced air-defense missile and rehearsed a fire strike. [14] The South China Morning Post reported it as the fourth weapons test in a week. [16]

Kim commissioned a second Choe Hyon-class destroyer at Wonsan on 6 September and called for a nuclear-armed navy. [13] He inspected the hull of what appears to be a cruiser of about 10,000 tons at Nampho on 2 November, and the Korea JoongAng Daily counted about 15 unveilings of conventional weapons between early September and early November. [17] NK News, relayed by Yonhap, reported satellite images of new warships under construction at Nampho and Chongjin. [18]

lenses.local: No independent reporting from inside the country exists on the nuclear program, and state media is the only domestic channel, as the reliance on KCNA in the coverage of the 4 November tests shows. [14]
lenses.international: AP and Al Jazeera carried the IAEA statement, and Stars and Stripes carried the 4 November launches. [5][14]
lenses.scholar: Vann Van Diepen's chapter in 38 North's summer briefing is titled North Korea Expanding Production of Uranium and Conventional Missiles. [19]

sections.title: Russia takes troops and shells and pays with money, food and technology, and a road bridge now joins the two
sections.body_md:
Pyongyang publicly acknowledged in April 2025 that it had sent troops to fight alongside Russia in Kursk, under a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty signed in June 2024. [20] On 26 April 2026 Kim told Russian Defence Minister Andrei Belousov he backed what he called a sacred war, at the opening of a Pyongyang memorial to North Korean dead. KCNA's account was relayed by AFP, which also reported that Belousov said Moscow was ready to sign a military cooperation plan for 2027 to 2031. [21]

The figures differ by source. South Korean intelligence estimated about 6,000 North Korean soldiers killed or wounded, with about 10,000 combat troops and 1,000 engineers in Kursk, according to Yonhap in February. [22] AFP in April quoted Seoul's estimate of about 2,000 killed. [21] Chatham House cites South Korea's Defence Intelligence Agency for more than 16,000 personnel sent since October 2024 and more than 15 million artillery rounds supplied. [20] A Ukrainian outlet citing Reuters reports that Ukrainian military intelligence put about 8,500 North Korean personnel in Russia in August, mostly guarding the border. [23] Zelenskyy suggested 30,000 to 50,000 more could deploy, Seoul sees no imminent move, and Kim Yo Jong called the claim groundless. [20][23]

The trade links are physical now. A Tumen River road bridge, about a kilometre long, opened to trucks on 7 September, with up to 300 vehicles a day expected, Reuters reported. [24] ASIAPRESS visited Fangchuan in October and saw new customs-style buildings at both ends. [25] Kim's aide Jo Yong Won was in Moscow in mid-November, where Putin said a monument to North Korean troops would be unveiled in Kursk this year. [26]

lenses.local: ASIAPRESS's reporters saw the new customs-style buildings at the Tumen bridge in October. [25]
lenses.international: Reuters, AFP and Yonhap carry the bridge opening, the April memorial and the November Moscow visit. [24][21][26]
lenses.scholar: Chatham House argues the partnership has become an institutional part of Moscow's war effort and will outlast the Ukraine war. [20]

sections.title: Trump asked for a meeting and got none, while Xi, Putin and Trump met in Shenzhen and Kim stayed home
sections.body_md:
Before leaving for the APEC summit in Shenzhen, Trump said Kim might come and that it was up to Xi, while a senior US official reportedly said no engagement was planned. [27] Trump left China on 19 November without meeting Kim, and the two have not met in person since June 2019. Newsis reported that Kim inspected sites in South Hamgyong province on 17 and 18 November. [3]

Trump, Xi and Putin held a three-way meeting at the summit and issued a declaration on nuclear risk reduction that did not mention the Korean Peninsula. Xinhua, a state outlet, later said the leaders discussed it. South Korean media worried that denuclearization was slipping down the agenda. [3] Kim Yo Jong rejected near-term dialogue after the FBI blamed North Korea for the Binance theft, calling the FBI's findings a "grave political provocation". [16] North Korea says there is no communication about a summit and that Washington must first drop its denuclearization demand, while the Trump administration wants to engage on the basis of the 2018 Singapore declaration. [13]

China is the other axis. Xi visited Pyongyang on 8 and 9 June, his first visit in seven years. CCTV, as relayed by AP, said both sides committed to deeper ties in trade, agriculture, construction and technology, and Kim called the friendship an unchanging strategic choice. [4] The New Yalu River Bridge opened in October after sitting unused for 12 years, though ASIAPRESS found light traffic at the Chinese customs site. [25]

lenses.local: ASIAPRESS reported light traffic at the Chinese customs site of the New Yalu River Bridge, which opened in October after 12 idle years. [25]
lenses.international: Euronews, Yonhap and AP report the Shenzhen summit, the missed meeting and Xi's June visit. [3][28][4]
lenses.scholar: Park Won-gon of Ewha Womans University called a Trump-Kim meeting at APEC particularly unlikely and said Kim may prefer working-level talks first. [27]

sections.title: Output is up 3.5 percent on paper while the won has lost about three quarters of its value
sections.body_md:
The Bank of Korea estimates North Korea's economy grew 3.5 percent in 2025, after 3.7 percent in 2024 and 3.1 percent in 2023. It credits cooperation with Russia, trade with China and regional development projects, with mining and manufacturing up 4.9 percent and construction up 6.3 percent. [29] Randall Jones of the Korea Economic Institute of America warns that the estimates need caution, since North Korea publishes no regular national accounts, and notes that China accounted for 98 percent of official trade in 2024. [30]

Household money tells a different story. 38 North reports that the market rate rose from about 37,250 won to the dollar in January to a peak near 70,800 in May, while tungsten ore exports to China rose from about $9 million to $88 million year on year over January to May. [31] Daily NK's survey recorded prices nearly doubling from early February to April, and rice at 38,200 won per kilogram in Pyongyang on 21 June, near a record. [33][1] Daily NK says its figures come from anonymous sources inside the country. [1]

ASIAPRESS's Rimjin-gang, using reporting partners at state grain stores in Ryanggang and North Hamgyong, found white rice at 38,500 won in mid-June 2026 against 5,600 in January 2023. A 50,000 won monthly wage bought 8.8 kg of white rice in January 2024 and 1.3 kg in June 2026. [2] The same outlet reported in January that three people in Musan County were sentenced to two years of labor correction for secretly selling about 3 tons of food, and in November that authorities are policing grain leaving rural areas after the harvest. [34][25] The FAO's September brief says satellite data showed generally good vegetation conditions in mid-August and gives no estimate of food insecurity. [35]

lenses.local: Daily NK and ASIAPRESS both describe collapsing purchasing power. Each relies on a few anonymous sources, and neither can be checked on the ground. [1][2]
lenses.international: Yonhap relays the Bank of Korea's 3.5 percent figure and its Russia and China drivers. [29]
lenses.scholar: 38 North argues that North Korea can still earn foreign exchange when world prices favor it but has lost control of its currency at home. [31]

sections.title: Executions are reported to be rising, escapes have nearly stopped and the UN calls it a human rights crisis
sections.body_md:
The Transitional Justice Working Group, a Seoul-based NGO, reported in April that it had confirmed 144 executions from 2011 to 2024, 65 of them after the border closed in 2020, and that executions and death sentences rose 116.7 percent over the following five years. Its findings draw on 265 defector testimonies and five media organizations with in-country contacts, and were not independently verified. [36] Amnesty's February report, based on 25 interviews with escapees, describes people facing execution for watching South Korean TV and bribes of $5,000 to $10,000 to escape punishment. It says a 2020 law sets 5 to 15 years of forced labor for watching or possessing South Korean media. Amnesty could not verify how widely the death penalty is used and received no reply from Pyongyang. [37]

UN Special Rapporteur Elizabeth Salmon told a General Assembly committee on 27 October that reports point to increased public executions, according to Human Rights Watch. [38] HRW says border guards remain under shoot-on-sight orders and that China forcibly returned at least 26 North Koreans in 2025, at least 1,076 since 2020. [40][39] UN High Commissioner Volker Turk called the situation a human rights crisis and said some violations may amount to crimes against humanity. [41] He urged an ICC referral on 16 March. [44]

Few can leave to tell it. Only 63 defectors reached South Korea in the first half of 2026, down 35 percent from 96 a year earlier, and Seoul's Unification Ministry blamed tighter controls on the China border. [43] ASIAPRESS reported in November that two men from Pochon County crossed the Yalu into China in late October, triggering a sweeping search and a crackdown on residents. [25]

lenses.local: ASIAPRESS's November feed describes a search and crackdown in Pochon County after two men fled. The item rests on the outlet's own sources and could not be confirmed. [25]
lenses.international: AFP reports that defections are in freefall as Kim seals the border and China tightens surveillance. [42]
lenses.scholar: HRW and the Transitional Justice Working Group both link a post-2020 rise in punishments to new laws on foreign media and say security talks should not push rights aside. [38][36]

sections.title: Sanctions monitoring now runs without the UN, and the largest crypto theft on record is blamed on Pyongyang
sections.body_md:
The UN Panel of Experts that monitored sanctions ended on 30 April 2024 after Russia vetoed its renewal, and Security Council members remain split on the file. [44] Eleven governments created the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team in October 2024. Its first report, on 29 May 2025, found that North Korea sent Russia at least 100 ballistic missiles in 2024 and that up to 9 million rounds moved in 49 shipments. [45] Some Council members feel the team lacks the authority of a Council body. [44]

Its September 2026 report on overseas labor estimates 35,600 to 101,280 North Korean workers abroad, almost all in China and Russia, earning $450 million to $800 million in 2025. It says the state seizes 80 to 90 percent of wages, that some workers in Russia reportedly make drones, and that Russia has used a student visa scheme to place them. [6]

On 31 October the FBI said North Korean actors were laundering a record $6.3 billion stolen from Binance, naming the group TraderTraitor, which it also blamed for the $1.5 billion Bybit theft. Binance says it has replaced 90 percent of the funds. [46] North Korea denies involvement, and Kim Yo Jong called the findings a grave political provocation. [16] The Rio Times reports that TRM Labs assigned the theft to the group with high confidence but has not published its evidence, and that reports differ on how much is frozen. [47] The US, EU and Australia recently imposed sanctions over North Korea's overseas workers, cyber activity and Russia cooperation. [14]

lenses.local: No reporting from inside the country covers hacking or the workers abroad. The wage and reprisal details in the MSMT statement come from defectors and other third parties. [6]
lenses.international: Reuters, via Al Jazeera, carries the FBI attribution and Binance's response, and Stars and Stripes carries the denial and the new sanctions. [46][14]
lenses.scholar: Security Council Report describes a divided Council in which China and Russia blame the US and its allies and argue for easing sanctions. [44]

timeline.text: The UN Panel of Experts on North Korea sanctions ends after Russia vetoes renewal.
Russia and North Korea sign a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty.
Pyongyang publicly acknowledges sending troops to fight alongside Russia in Kursk.
The MSMT publishes its first report, on North Korea-Russia arms transfers.
The Ninth Party Congress opens in Pyongyang.
A third round of constitutional revisions is reflected in a text later surfaced in South Korea.
Kim meets Russia's defence minister at the opening of a memorial to North Korean troops.
Xi Jinping visits Pyongyang, his first visit in seven years.
The Bank of Korea estimates 3.5 percent growth for 2025.
A Tumen River road bridge to Russia opens to trucks.
The MSMT publishes its report on North Korea's overseas labor program.
Two explosions near the western DMZ wound three South Korean soldiers.
The FBI attributes a record $6.3 billion Binance theft to North Korean actors.
North Korea tests an air-defense missile and rehearses a fire strike; Seoul detects missile launches.
The IAEA says a new extension at Yongbyon's enrichment plant is externally complete.
Trump leaves the APEC summit in China without meeting Kim.

scores.coverage_basis: AP, Reuters and AFP file on North Korea regularly, including the IAEA statement on Yongbyon, the Xi visit, the Tumen bridge and the Binance attribution [5][4][24][46]. Specialist output is steady, with 38 North's quarterly briefings and daily Daily NK reporting [19][1]. Coverage of daily life, hunger and rights is far thinner than coverage of missiles because on-the-ground reporting is impossible [42].

severity.basis: North Korean troops fight in Russia, with Seoul's estimates ranging from about 2,000 killed to about 6,000 killed or wounded, and two DMZ explosions wounded three South Korean soldiers in September [21][22][48].
Rice cost 38,200 won per kg in June and a monthly wage bought 1.3 kg of white rice, per exile outlets, while no UN hunger count exists [1][2][35].
The UN rights chief calls the situation a human rights crisis, border guards have shoot-on-sight orders, and the TJWG reports executions up 116.7 percent after 2020 [41][40][36].
The won lost about three quarters of its dollar value since May 2024 and rice rose 5.2 times, though the Bank of Korea estimates 3.5 percent growth under sanctions [30][29].
Executions and prices are reported rising and Yongbyon is expanding, but the state sector is growing with Russian and Chinese support [36][5][29].

parts.basis: Russia has North Korean troops, shells and a new road bridge, China is its main trade partner and Xi visited in June, and Washington is seeking a Kim meeting [20][24][4][27].

North Korea supplies Russia with munitions and the FBI attributes a record $6.3 billion crypto theft to it, but its economy is about 1.8 percent the size of South Korea's and its official trade is mostly with China [20][46][29][30].
An expanding enrichment plant, repeated missile tests and DMZ mine incidents sit beside troop deployments to a European war [5][14][48][20].
The MSMT estimates 35,600 to 101,280 North Korean workers abroad, and about 34,600 defectors live in South Korea [6][43].
Pyongyang demands recognition as a nuclear state, the UN Panel of Experts was ended by a Russian veto and sanctions monitoring moved to an 11-government team [10][44].

summary: North Korea matters beyond its borders through its nuclear program, its role as a supplier and troop provider in Russia's war, and the erosion of the sanctions system, more than through trade [5][20][44].
gi.up: Recognition of North Korea as a nuclear state by Washington, a new nuclear test, or a further large troop deployment to Russia.
gi.down: A verifiable freeze at Yongbyon, a restored UN monitoring panel, or an end to Russia's war that cuts the arms and troop trade.

gaps: No independent local reporting is possible inside North Korea. The local lens rests on exile and cross-border outlets (Daily NK in Seoul, Rimjin-gang/ASIAPRESS in Osaka) whose reports come from a few anonymous in-country contacts and cannot be checked on the ground. Every local source is flagged single_sourced.

KCNA, Rodong Sinmun and other DPRK state media were not cited directly. Pyongyang's statements reach this draft through AFP, Yonhap, Reuters and Stars and Stripes, and Chinese state media (CCTV, Xinhua) through AP and Euronews. Treat them as state-affiliated claims.
NK News articles could not be opened (the site was not fetchable here). NK News appears only through a Yonhap relay and podcast listings.

Daily NK's late-November headlines (phone inspections in Chongjin, Hyesan children hauling water, fuel payments from Russia) were seen only as headlines on its home page; the articles were not opened.
The Rimjin-gang November items were read from feed summaries only.

Crisis Group's North Korea page showed no dated 2026 publications, CSIS's China-North Korea analysis could not be loaded, and CSIS Beyond Parallel's February panel page reports no findings. No 2026 Carnegie analysis was read. 38 North (Stimson) is the main think tank source.

The MSMT reports were read through a joint government statement and press coverage, not the reports themselves. The UN Panel of Experts has not existed since April 2024, so there is no UN-mandated count of sanctions violations.

No food insecurity or IPC figure for 2026 exists in the sources read. FAO's page gave crop conditions only, and WFP and other UN agencies have no current in-country data in this draft. The hunger picture rests on market prices from Daily NK and ASIAPRESS.

Troop casualty and deployment figures conflict (about 2,000 killed per Seoul in April, about 6,000 killed or wounded per Yonhap in February, 8,500 in Russia per Ukrainian intelligence via a Ukrainian outlet citing Reuters). The Ukrainian figure is second hand.

The Binance attribution rests on the FBI and TRM Labs, whose evidence is unpublished, and was read through Reuters (via Al Jazeera) and a secondary aggregator. Reports differ on funds frozen or replaced.

The constitution text and its 2026 revisions come from a 38 North page with no author or date shown; Pyongyang never published the text in full. The Ju Ae succession assessment is a second-hand account of a closed briefing.

Amnesty's and the TJWG's findings rest on defector testimony, much of it from people who left before or around 2020. The Bank of Korea growth figure is an estimate; the underlying accounts are not public.
No documentary, photo essay or film was verified, so the media list is empty. Two podcast episodes were verified from a feed page that gives relative dates.
Health, disaster, abductee and Japan-related issues are not covered in this draft.

local_md:
Daily NK's analysis of the congress, drawn from its own report, calls the result "Kim Jong Un regime 2.0" and says military figures Ri Pyong Chol and Pak Jong Chon lost Party standing. [8]

No independent reporting from inside the country exists on the nuclear program, and state media is the only domestic channel, as the reliance on KCNA in the coverage of the 4 November tests shows. [14]

ASIAPRESS's reporters saw the new customs-style buildings at the Tumen bridge in October. [25]

ASIAPRESS reported light traffic at the Chinese customs site of the New Yalu River Bridge, which opened in October after 12 idle years. [25]

Daily NK and ASIAPRESS both describe collapsing purchasing power. Each relies on a few anonymous sources, and neither can be checked on the ground. [1][2]

ASIAPRESS's November feed describes a search and crackdown in Pochon County after two men fled. The item rests on the outlet's own sources and could not be confirmed. [25]

No reporting from inside the country covers hacking or the workers abroad. The wage and reprisal details in the MSMT statement come from defectors and other third parties. [6]
international_md:
Al Jazeera, citing Yonhap, noted that Kim did not mention relations with the US or South Korea in his opening speech. [9]

AP and Al Jazeera carried the IAEA statement, and Stars and Stripes carried the 4 November launches. [5][14]

Reuters, AFP and Yonhap carry the bridge opening, the April memorial and the November Moscow visit. [24][21][26]

Euronews, Yonhap and AP report the Shenzhen summit, the missed meeting and Xi's June visit. [3][28][4]

Yonhap relays the Bank of Korea's 3.5 percent figure and its Russia and China drivers. [29]

AFP reports that defections are in freefall as Kim seals the border and China tightens surveillance. [42]

Reuters, via Al Jazeera, carries the FBI attribution and Binance's response, and Stars and Stripes carries the denial and the new sanctions. [46][14]
scholar_md:
Vann Van Diepen expects nuclear weapons production to continue, and Gyeong Seob Oh sees no concrete economic reforms or sanctions relief in the five-year plan. [7]

Vann Van Diepen's chapter in 38 North's summer briefing is titled North Korea Expanding Production of Uranium and Conventional Missiles. [19]

Chatham House argues the partnership has become an institutional part of Moscow's war effort and will outlast the Ukraine war. [20]

Park Won-gon of Ewha Womans University called a Trump-Kim meeting at APEC particularly unlikely and said Kim may prefer working-level talks first. [27]

38 North argues that North Korea can still earn foreign exchange when world prices favor it but has lost control of its currency at home. [31]

HRW and the Transitional Justice Working Group both link a post-2020 rise in punishments to new laws on foreign media and say security talks should not push rights aside. [38][36]

Security Council Report describes a divided Council in which China and Russia blame the US and its allies and argue for easing sanctions. [44]
